The method provides a substrate suitable for epitaxial growth that exhibits improved biaxial crystal orientation while suppressing the formation of irregular regions. In this method, a metal base material is laminated with a copper layer having a face-centered cubic (FCC) rolling texture. The lamination is performed by surface-activated bonding, which enables the two materials to be joined without substantially disturbing the desired texture of the copper layer.

After lamination, the copper layer is mechanically polished and then subjected to an orientation heat treatment to enhance its crystallographic alignment. To maintain the required texture, the copper layer must exhibit, both before and after lamination, an X-ray diffraction (XRD) intensity ratio of less than 20% for the (200) plane and between 70% and 90% for the (220) plane. In addition, the increase in the (200) plane XRD ratio caused by lamination must be less than 13 percentage points. Controlling these parameters limits undesirable changes in crystal orientation during bonding and helps produce a uniform substrate with improved biaxial orientation for subsequent epitaxial growth.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for manufacturing an epitaxial-growth substrate having a highly uniform biaxial crystal orientation and substantially no regions of disturbed or irregular orientation. The method uses a metal base material and a copper layer having a rolling texture and a face-centered-cubic crystal structure. Bonding surfaces of the metal base material and the copper layer are activated, for example by removing surface contaminants and oxide films under reduced pressure, and the activated surfaces are then brought into contact and pressure-bonded. This surface-activated bonding process enables firm lamination without introducing an intervening layer that could impair crystallographic alignment.

After bonding, the exposed surface of the copper layer is mechanically polished to remove surface unevenness and deformation and to obtain a smooth surface suitable for epitaxial growth. The laminated body is subsequently subjected to an orientation heat treatment. This treatment promotes recovery and recrystallization of the rolling-textured copper layer, thereby improving both the in-plane and out-of-plane alignment of its crystal grains while suppressing the formation of locally misoriented regions.

The crystallographic condition of the copper layer is controlled using X-ray diffraction measurements. In particular, the intensity ratio \(I_0\), representing undesired or irregular orientation components, is maintained below 20%. The intensity ratio \(I_2\), representing the desired biaxially oriented component, is maintained within the range of 70% to 90% both before and after lamination. In addition, the increase in \(I_0\) caused by the lamination process is limited to less than 13 percentage points. Controlling these diffraction-intensity ratios prevents substantial degradation of the rolling texture during bonding and subsequent processing.

As a result, the finished substrate has a smooth surface, strong adhesion between the copper layer and the metal base, and a more uniform and highly developed biaxial crystal orientation. The suppression of irregularly oriented regions makes the substrate particularly suitable for forming epitaxial functional layers, including superconducting, semiconductor, magnetic, or other crystalline thin films whose performance depends on consistent crystallographic alignment.
outputs.L5:
# The Role of XRD in Material Analysis

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) technique is widely used to investigate the crystalline structure of materials. By directing X-rays onto a sample and measuring the resulting diffraction patterns, XRD can identify crystalline phases, determine lattice parameters, and estimate crystallite size. The technique is valuable in fields such as geology, chemistry, pharmaceuticals, metallurgy, and materials science.

XRD is generally non-destructive and can analyze powders, thin films, and bulk materials. The diffraction pattern produced by each crystalline substance acts like a unique fingerprint, allowing researchers to identify unknown compounds and evaluate their purity. As a result, XRD is an essential tool for material characterization, quality control, and scientific research.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description of a copper-clad substrate manufacturing process in which I0Cu and I0CLAD are below 20%, I2Cu and I2CLAD are 70–90%, and I0CLAD−I0Cu is less than 13%.
counterfactuals.output:
### Copper-Clad Substrate Manufacturing Process

A copper-clad substrate is manufactured by preparing a copper foil and a substrate, activating the opposing bonding surfaces, and laminating the copper foil to the substrate under controlled temperature and pressure. The process is regulated so that the measured indices \(I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}\), \(I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\), \(I2_{\mathrm{Cu}}\), and \(I2_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\) satisfy:

\[
I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}<20\%, \qquad I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}<20\%
\]

\[
70\%\le I2_{\mathrm{Cu}}\le90\%, \qquad
70\%\le I2_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\le90\%
\]

and

\[
I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}-I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}<13\text{ percentage points}.
\]

The indices for the copper foil before cladding and for the copper layer after cladding are determined using the same sampling geometry, specimen-conditioning procedure, and analytical method.

The copper foil is first degreased and cleaned to remove rolling oil, oxides, and particulates. At least the bonding surface may then be mechanically, chemically, or electrochemically roughened. Surface treatment is controlled to produce a substantially uniform bonding topography without excessive cold work or preferential removal of selected surface regions. An adhesion-promoting layer, such as a silane, metal-oxide, conversion-coating, or resin-compatible primer, may be applied in an amount that does not materially interfere with measurement of the indices.

The substrate may comprise a thermosetting or thermoplastic dielectric sheet, a fiber-reinforced prepreg, a ceramic-containing dielectric, or another dimensionally stable core. The treated copper foil is positioned against the substrate and consolidated by hot pressing, continuous lamination, or roll bonding. Lamination temperature, pressure, line speed or dwell time, and cooling rate are selected to limit changes in the copper condition during cladding. In particular, excessive deformation, uncontrolled recrystallization, and nonuniform thermal exposure are avoided because they can raise \(I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\), lower \(I2_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\), or increase the difference between \(I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\) and \(I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}\).

Where necessary, the copper foil is subjected to a pre-lamination recovery or annealing treatment so that \(I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}\) is below 20% and \(I2_{\mathrm{Cu}}\) is within 70–90% before assembly. A post-lamination thermal treatment may also be used, provided that it maintains \(I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\) below 20%, maintains \(I2_{\mathrm{CLAD}}\) within 70–90%, and keeps \(I0_{\mathrm{CLAD}}-I0_{\mathrm{Cu}}\) below 13 percentage points.

Process qualification is performed by measuring representative samples of the incoming copper foil and corresponding regions of the finished copper-clad substrate. Lots falling outside any of the specified ranges are reprocessed, where permissible, or rejected. Maintaining the stated relationships provides a clad copper layer whose measured condition remains close to that of the starting foil while limiting formation of the population represented by \(I0\) and retaining a predominant \(I2\) population.
